explainers.title: Why the Sun stays low at the pole

captions.text: The Moon spins standing almost straight up, like a top.
So at the south pole, sunlight comes in from the side.
The Sun never climbs. It rolls around the edge of the sky.
Here is how high the Sun gets in 2046 and 2047. Zero is the horizon.
It stays between −1.56° and +1.59°: just a peek above or below.
That is smaller than your thumb held out at arm's length!
So up high is best. A tall crater rim can stay sunny 240 days straight.
Down in the crater it stays dark. Even on the rim, darkness can last 1.5 days.

explainers.ends_on: Sunlight here comes and goes. In the dark shifts, the base runs on its battery alone.

explainers.title: Reading a proton-flux chart

captions.text: A weather satellite near Earth counts tiny, fast bits of the Sun: protons.
Its count is in pfu: protons per square centimetre, each second.
On a normal scale, a quiet day is so small you cannot even see it.
On a log scale, each step up is ten times bigger. Now both fit!
10 September 2017: an X8.2 flare bursts on the Sun at 15:35 UTC.
At 16:45 UTC, the protons cross the storm line: 10 pfu.
That is just seventy minutes after the flare began.
Then they stay high for days, peaking at 1,493.5 pfu!
The Moon has no air or magnetic shield, so storms like this reach the ground.

explainers.ends_on: When the alarm sounds, the protons are already on their way. Get the shelter ready before it!
